Once irrelevant pixels enter the same unit as the useful detail, the system has to compare a mixed signal. Attention, meaning learned weighting of which pieces should count more, can reduce noise, but it still starts from pieces that may already be poorly drawn. The paper's central tension is therefore shape mismatch: the search target is a fine visual attribute, while the default units are coarse squares that can blur the attribute with background.
383.naive: A smart beginner would crop or resize every fashion image, divide it into equal patches, turn each patch into a description, and compare images by how strongly their patch descriptions match the requested attribute. This can work for large, centered cues such as overall color or garment type. It fails for attribute-specific search because the patch grid is blind to garment boundaries. One patch may contain half a pocket and half a plain fabric region; another may contain the edge of a collar plus background. The beginner might then assign higher weight to patches that seem attribute-related, but the patch still remains a bad container. Weighting a noisy rectangle cannot fully recover the pixel-level microstructure that was mixed away when the image was chopped into squares.
383.ap: The core idea is to build the comparison units from the image itself. Super Fashion first uses attribute-guided attention, a learned focusing step directed by the requested attribute, to find image features related to that attribute. Those features guide cropping, so the system works on semantically meaningful image regions instead of the full photo. Within those regions, it applies superpixel segmentation. A superpixel is a compact group of nearby pixels that look coherent in color or texture, so its boundary can follow an irregular garment part better than a fixed rectangle. The system then treats both the attribute description and these superpixel groups as tokens, meaning small information units passed into a Transformer. It gives the attribute units and superpixel units different type labels, then lets them interact so the model can decide which visual pieces best express the requested fashion attribute.
383.mech: The mechanism starts with a fashion image and an attribute retrieval need. First, an attribute-guided attention module extracts features related to the target attribute. In plain terms, it scans the image representation and gives stronger influence to locations that look relevant to the requested detail. Those selected features guide a crop, narrowing the field from the whole product photo to image regions that are more likely to contain meaningful garment evidence. Second, the cropped regions are segmented into superpixels. This replaces a fixed square grid with image-shaped pieces: small coherent pixel groups that can trace fabric texture, edge shape, or local structure more closely. Third, each superpixel group is converted into a compact token, a small package of numbers that carries information about that image piece. The attribute is also represented as tokens. Fourth, the model marks the two token types with modality-specific embeddings, which are type labels in numeric form that tell the Transformer whether a unit came from the attribute side or the superpixel image side. Finally, the Transformer lets these units exchange influence. It compares, combines, and refines them so attribute evidence can point to the right visual pieces and visual pieces can sharpen the attribute match. The output is a representation used to localize the attribute and discriminate between candidate fashion images for retrieval.
383.math: The main mathematical idea is selective comparison. Retrieval needs a way to put candidate images in an order, so the system must turn each image and requested attribute into comparable descriptions. Similarity is the act of deciding what counts as close: here, closeness should mean sharing the same attribute-specific visual detail, not merely sharing background, pose, or general garment type. Attention is weighted combining: the model gives different amounts of influence to different image locations because only some locations are relevant to the attribute. Superpixel segmentation adds a geometric prior, a built-in assumption about shape: nearby pixels that look alike often belong to the same meaningful visual piece. That prior matters because the target evidence is irregular and local. The Transformer then performs repeated weighted exchange among tokens. Each token updates itself by listening more to related tokens and less to unrelated ones. The modality-specific labels solve a bookkeeping problem: attribute units and image-region units carry different kinds of evidence, so the model should know their source before mixing them. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Superpixels save the system from processing every pixel separately, but each superpixel still compresses many pixels into one unit. The method works only if that compression preserves the attribute microstructure that retrieval needs.
383.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas. It is a retrieval paper because the final practical act is ranking a large pile of fashion images so the few best matches rise to the top. It is also a similarity paper because the system must learn what kind of visual nearness matters for a specific attribute. Two dresses can be visually close in color but far apart in collar shape; another pair can differ in background yet match in sleeve structure. The work also belongs to multimodal vision-language reasoning in the repo's family data, because attribute evidence and image-region evidence are different channels that must be aligned before a decision. Its use of attention connects it to the broader selective-influence idea: not every region, patch, or feature deserves equal say. Compared with generic image retrieval, the narrower pressure here is fine-grained localization. The paper is a sibling of methods that replace one coarse representation with task-shaped pieces, then rank candidates using the pieces most tied to the user's intent.
383.ww: The method should improve over the patch-based approach because it changes the unit of evidence before comparison begins. If the unit is a square patch, then a curved neckline and its surrounding background may be fused from the start. Later weighting can reduce the damage, but it still has to reason from a contaminated unit. If the unit is a superpixel inside an attribute-guided crop, the piece is more likely to contain coherent garment evidence. That gives the later Transformer cleaner things to compare. The attribute-guided crop also reduces the search area, so background noise has fewer chances to compete with the detail. The type labels for attribute and superpixel tokens help the model avoid treating words or attribute cues and visual regions as identical evidence; instead, it can learn how one should guide the other. In intuitive terms, the paper first asks where the requested detail probably lives, then redraws the image into local pieces that follow the detail, and only then compares candidates. That order fits the problem better than comparing square chunks of the whole scene.
383.po: The payoff is more accurate fine-grained fashion retrieval for web image search. According to the abstract, experiments on FashionAI, DARN, and DeepFashion show relative overall MAP improvements of 1.84%, 9.27%, and 9.35% over prior state-of-the-art methods. MAP is a ranking measure that rewards placing relevant images earlier in the result list, so the reported gains mean the system is better at moving attribute-matching items upward. The practical capability is not just recognizing a garment category. It is retrieving items that match subtle attribute regions, where pixel-level texture and irregular local shape matter.
383.limits: The abstract supports the mechanism and reported benchmark gains, but it does not prove deployment reliability across all fashion sites. The method assumes the attribute-guided attention can crop meaningful regions; if that first focusing step misses the attribute, later superpixels are built in the wrong place. It also assumes superpixel boundaries preserve the important visual structure rather than splitting or merging it poorly under shadows, unusual poses, cluttered backgrounds, or low-quality product images. The reported evidence comes from FashionAI, DARN, and DeepFashion, so behavior on new catalogs, rare attributes, different photography styles, or ambiguous user queries remains an assumption. The abstract also does not state the added computation cost of segmentation and Transformer interaction.

384.bp: Crowdsourced labeling is the work behind many machine learning systems: people mark images, text, audio, or video so a later model can learn what counts as the right answer. The platform has a practical problem before any algorithm appears. It needs many workers, but it cannot treat every submitted label as equally helpful. Some workers are careful, some are inexperienced, and some may deliberately submit bad labels or try to earn payment with minimal effort. If bad labels enter the training pile, the later model learns from corrupted examples. If the platform punishes too harshly, honest workers may avoid participating. This paper serves that tension. It proposes a Negativity-Aware Incentive mechanism for paying and penalizing workers according to whether their actual labeling behavior helps or harms the final data quality, with reported deployment evidence from NetEase Youling.
384.wh: The hard part is that label quality is both a measurement problem and a human incentives problem. A platform does not directly observe effort or honesty; it sees submitted answers, worker history, task difficulty, and later agreement or result quality. Existing methods, according to the abstract, often ignore fraud or assume worker utility is never negative. That means they can reward good work but have trouble assigning real cost to harmful work. Yet penalty design is dangerous. If every mistake is treated as fraud, new or lower-ability workers may leave. If no mistake carries a cost, malicious or careless workers can damage the dataset while still being paid. The system must therefore separate helpful from harmful contribution, attach money to that separation, and keep the rule fair enough that ordinary workers still want to join. It also has to work across different media types and at real platform scale.
384.naive: A smart beginner would pay workers per completed task and remove workers who fail too many gold-standard checks. That is simple and easy to explain. It fails because completion is not the same as contribution. A worker can submit many labels that look complete while adding noise or fraud. Another beginner plan is to pay according to average accuracy. That helps, but it can miss the effect of a specific worker on a specific task result, especially when task difficulty and worker ability differ. A third plan is to apply fixed fines for bad answers. That can discourage fraud, but it can also scare off honest workers who make occasional mistakes or face harder items.
384.ap: The core idea is to make contribution signed: a worker can add value, add little value, or subtract value. The paper's Ability-Result Characteristic Function combines two pieces of evidence, the worker's ability and the real-time task result, to define how much that worker contributed. It adapts Shapley value theory, which is a way of dividing credit among people who jointly produce an outcome, so that the division can include blame as well as reward. The second move is economic. Workers participate through a dynamic stake pool, meaning some value is committed in advance and later adjusted. Adaptive dual-control parameters tune the balance between fairness and operating efficiency. In concrete terms, NAI tries to make the price of fraud visible while still letting useful workers earn and continue participating.
384.mech: The mechanism starts with a labeling task and a set of workers who produce answers for that task. For each worker, the system keeps evidence about ability, meaning how reliable that worker appears to be, and it also observes the current task result rather than judging only from a static profile. These ingredients enter the Ability-Result Characteristic Function. A characteristic function, in this setting, is a rule that says what value a group of workers appears to create for the labeling outcome. The paper extends this rule so value can be positive or negative. Next, a Shapley-style calculation asks a fairness question: if workers were added to the group in different possible orders, how much did this worker tend to change the outcome? A worker whose labels move the result toward quality receives positive contribution. A worker whose behavior damages the result receives negative contribution. That signed contribution then feeds the incentive side. The dynamic stake pool uses pre-commitment economics: workers have something at risk before final payment is settled. The adaptive controls change how strongly rewards and penalties are applied so the platform can punish harmful behavior without making the system too costly or hostile. The output is a payment and penalty decision tied to measured contribution, plus a higher-quality labeled dataset.
384.math: The first mathematical idea is cooperative credit assignment. When several people label the same data, the platform needs more than a count of who participated; it needs a fair estimate of each person's marginal effect, meaning the difference that person tends to make when added to others. Shapley value theory gives a disciplined way to divide credit by averaging a person's added value across many possible groupings. The paper changes the usual use by allowing the value to be signed. Positive numbers mean the worker helped; negative numbers mean the worker harmed the result. That matters because fraud is not merely absence of help. It can actively lower data quality. The second idea is a payoff rule with incentives. A payoff rule changes behavior because people react to expected reward and loss. Pre-commitment makes that loss credible: a worker has something at stake before the outcome is judged. The third idea is control under a tradeoff. The adaptive dual controls tune penalty and reward strength, balancing fairness against operational efficiency. Too little penalty leaves fraud cheap. Too much penalty treats noise as guilt and discourages participation. The math fits because the problem is not just classifying labels as right or wrong; it is assigning credit and blame among many contributors whose actions jointly determine a dataset.
384.dots: This paper connects crowdsourcing incentives to several recurring conference ideas. It belongs near fraud and anomaly detection because it treats harmful worker behavior as a pattern that must be made costly, not merely observed after damage is done. It also connects to fairness and responsible AI because the payment rule must avoid confusing low ability, task difficulty, and deliberate fraud; a punishment system that cannot make that distinction would be unfair even if it improves average quality. The Shapley value link places the paper in the broader family of contribution measurement, where systems ask how to divide credit among people, data sources, model components, or agents that jointly produce an outcome. Its economic side connects to mechanism design: instead of only predicting behavior, the system changes the rules of participation so honest labeling becomes more attractive than harmful labeling. The multimodal datasets show that the issue is not tied to one data type.
384.ww: The approach should work better than flat payment because it changes what workers are being paid for. A flat rule buys completed actions. NAI tries to buy useful contribution. If a worker's answer improves the task result, the signed contribution score can reward that effect. If the answer harms the result, the same scoring language can assign a negative value rather than pretending the worker merely contributed less. That is important because fraud is active damage. The stake pool then turns the score into an incentive before behavior happens: workers know that harmful contributions can cost them, so careless or fraudulent strategies become less attractive. At the same time, the ability-result design gives the system more evidence than a single wrong answer. It can combine a worker's ability with real-time task outcomes, which should reduce the chance that honest mistakes are punished like deliberate attacks. The abstract's reported gains across images, text, audio, and video suggest the mechanism is using a general property of crowdsourcing: quality improves when money follows measured contribution rather than task volume alone.
384.po: The payoff is a labeling market that can reward careful workers and penalize harmful contributors inside the same rule. The abstract reports extensive experiments on image, text, audio, and video datasets, including a 16.6% improvement in video labeling accuracy and a 33.9% reduction in fraudulent behavior against baselines. It also reports deployment on NetEase Youling, with 430,000 registered workers and 80,000 monthly active workers. In real-time A/B testing, NAI improved labeling quality by 59.6% for beginner tasks and reduced fraud rates by 14.8% to 33.9% across difficulty levels. The practical capability is better data quality without relying only on manual policing.
384.limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The system must estimate worker ability and task results well enough that signed contribution is meaningful. If the result signal is noisy, biased, or delayed, a good worker could be penalized or a harmful worker could escape cost. The stake pool must be acceptable to workers; otherwise the mechanism may improve quality among remaining workers while driving away useful participants. The abstract reports strong deployment evidence, but it does not show every detail of worker experience, appeal processes, long-term adaptation by fraudsters, or how penalties behave on rare hard tasks. The method also assumes money-based incentives are the right lever for the platform setting.

385.bp: A recommender system is trying to choose useful items for people from a very large catalog. The raw evidence is usually a record of interactions: this user clicked, bought, rated, watched, or ignored that item. The paper starts from two ordinary failures in that record. First, most possible user-item pairs are empty, so the system sees only a few clues in a huge table. Second, the clues are uneven: common items, common behaviors, or majority interaction types can dominate, while rare but important cases get too little evidence. The paper's real object is therefore not just a user or an item, but the interaction itself. It asks whether each observed user-item connection can be treated as something we can classify, balance, and augment. By turning the original user-item map into a line graph, LGDA gives recommendation a different workbench: one where methods for scarce and imbalanced node labels can be used to create better training evidence.
385.wh: The hard part is that recommendation data is thin in exactly the places where the system needs confidence. A person may interact with only a tiny fraction of all items, and many items may receive little attention. If the model learns mostly from frequent interactions, it can become good at repeating what is already well represented while missing weaker signals for less common users, items, or labels. Class imbalance adds a second pressure: if one kind of signal greatly outnumbers another, a learner can look accurate by favoring the majority and still fail on the minority cases that matter for personalization. The abstract's key insight is that these are not only recommendation problems; they can be seen as graph learning problems after a change of viewpoint. But that shift must be done carefully. A transformed graph can expose new structure, yet it can also create noisy candidate additions if the augmentation step trusts uncertain connections too easily.
385.naive: A smart beginner would try to fix sparse recommendation data by adding more examples directly to the user-item table. They might duplicate rare interactions, sample fewer common interactions, or invent new user-item pairs that look plausible because similar users touched similar items. This can help counts look more balanced, but it does not explain which new examples deserve trust. Duplicating rare cases can make the model memorize accidental patterns. Inventing interactions in the original table can accidentally say that a user liked an item when the evidence only showed a weak neighborhood hint. The beginner is trying to repair missing evidence at the same level where the data is already sparse. LGDA instead changes the object being repaired: it treats interactions as nodes in a new graph, then augments there with confidence filtering.
385.ap: The core move is to turn the user-item interaction graph inside out. In the original bipartite graph, users sit on one side, items sit on the other, and an edge means a user interacted with an item. A line graph makes each original edge into a node. Two new nodes are connected when their original interactions are related, such as sharing a user or sharing an item. After this transformation, the question changes. Sparse interactions become insufficient labeled nodes in the line graph, and uneven interaction types become an imbalanced label distribution over those nodes. That reformulation matters because node classification and imbalanced graph learning already have tools for spreading evidence, adding targeted examples, and filtering uncertain additions. LGDA uses this route as a module placed around an existing recommender, aiming to supply higher-quality, more balanced augmented data without changing the recommender's own design.
385.mech: The input is a user-item interaction bipartite graph: users, items, and the observed links between them. LGDA first builds the line graph. Every observed interaction becomes a node in this new graph. If two interactions are structurally related in the original graph, the corresponding line-graph nodes are linked, so evidence can be compared through shared users, shared items, or similar interaction context. The paper then treats each interaction-node as something that may have a label, and the old sparsity problem becomes a shortage of labeled nodes in this new graph. The imbalance problem becomes an uneven count of labels across these interaction-nodes. From there, LGDA can use mature node classification and imbalanced graph learning ideas: estimate which unlabeled or underrepresented interaction-nodes look reliable, focus augmentation on the weak parts of the label distribution, and avoid simply flooding the data with easy majority cases. Its confidence filtering step is important because augmentation is only useful if the new examples are likely to be correct. Low-confidence generated cases are removed rather than handed to the recommender as training truth. The output is a more balanced set of augmented interaction data. That output is then fed into the underlying recommendation model as an external module, so the base recommender can benefit from better evidence without being redesigned.
385.math: The main mathematical object is a graph: a map of things and relationships. In the original map, the things are users and items, and the relationships are interactions. In the line graph, the things are the interactions themselves. This is a mathematical change of viewpoint, not just a data-format trick. It asks, "Which interactions are neighbors of other interactions?" rather than only "Which user touched which item?" That matters because graph methods can move evidence through relationships. If two interaction-nodes are connected, one may provide a clue about the other, though the method must decide how much to trust that clue. The second idea is classification: assigning labels to nodes from partial examples. Here, the labels stand for the categories the augmented data must balance. The third idea is imbalance handling: changing the learning process so that rare labels are not drowned out by common ones. The tradeoff is signal versus noise. Adding examples can reduce scarcity, but careless additions can teach false patterns. Confidence filtering is a probability-like guard: it keeps cases whose evidence looks strong enough and discards cases whose estimated label is too uncertain. The math fits because the problem is about connected, uneven evidence, not isolated records.
385.dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems family because it tries to improve the small set of items shown to a user when the past record is incomplete. It also belongs to the graph-learning thread: like other network papers in the repo, it assumes relationships carry useful evidence when single records are too thin. The line-graph step is a particularly direct bridge between those families, because it makes an interaction into a node that can receive graph-based treatment. It connects to ranking because the eventual recommender still has to sort candidate items; LGDA works earlier, repairing the evidence used to learn that sorting. It connects to probability and learning from examples because confidence filtering asks whether a generated case is trustworthy enough to become training data. Compared with papers that fight popularity bias, long-tail item weakness, cold-start histories, or noisy recommendation explanations, this one attacks a lower-level data problem: the training graph itself gives too few and too uneven examples before ranking even begins.
385.ww: LGDA should help over the naive approach because it uses the structure around an interaction before deciding how to augment it. In the original user-item table, a missing or rare interaction is just an empty cell or a lonely example. In the line graph, that same interaction can be compared with neighboring interactions that share users, items, or surrounding graph patterns. This gives the method more context for deciding which scarce labels need support and which candidate additions look believable. Targeted augmentation addresses the imbalance directly: the goal is not merely to make the dataset bigger, but to strengthen underrepresented parts of the evidence. Confidence filtering then reduces the main danger of synthetic data, which is treating guesses as facts. The plug-in design also helps because the recommender itself does not have to be rebuilt around a new architecture. If the line-graph reformulation produces cleaner, better balanced training examples, many underlying recommenders can learn less from majority accidents and more from previously weak interaction signals.
385.po: The payoff is a practical way to reduce two persistent recommendation failures at once: sparse user-item evidence and imbalanced interaction labels. The abstract reports that LGDA is a plug-and-play module, so its value is not tied to replacing the underlying recommendation model. It reformulates the problem into a line-graph domain, uses targeted augmentation plus confidence filtering, and produces balanced augmented data for training. Experiments on four real-world datasets are reported to show improved recommendation performance and greater stability under the sparsity and imbalance conditions the paper targets. The practical capability is better use of thin interaction records without asking every recommender designer to build a specialized sparse-data method from scratch.
385.limits: The abstract does not specify exactly how related interactions are connected in the line graph, how confidence is computed, or which base recommenders and datasets were tested. The method assumes that the line graph preserves useful neighborhood information: interactions near each other in the transformed graph must genuinely share preference evidence, not just popularity or exposure bias. It also assumes the labels used for augmentation are meaningful and that confidence filtering can separate helpful generated cases from misleading ones. If rare interactions are rare because they are noisy, accidental, or caused by platform exposure rather than user preference, adding more of them could mislead the model. The reported four-dataset evidence supports the claim, but the abstract does not prove the same behavior across all domains, feedback types, or deployment settings.

386.bp: This entry is not trying to solve one narrow prediction task. It is trying to build a place where the web research community can examine how it judges its own tools. Web technology now includes social network analysis, graph algorithms, web mining, semantics and knowledge, security, privacy, fairness, and ethics. Those areas produce models, datasets, and practical systems, but a reader often needs more than another isolated result. They need careful guides that say what a model is for, what a dataset leaves out, which comparisons are fair, and which claims survive contact with practice. TIME 2026 serves that need by inviting survey, evaluation, and review papers that critically analyze models and datasets from several perspectives. The real object being improved is the community's shared map of evidence: what is known, what is uncertain, and what practitioners or newcomers can responsibly use.
386.wh: The hard part is that evaluation in web research is not one measurement with one answer. A graph algorithm may look good on speed but poor on fairness. A privacy method may hide sensitive facts but make a system less useful. A dataset may be convenient while quietly excluding important groups or real deployment conditions. A beginner might hope that a leaderboard, a famous dataset, or a single accuracy number can settle the matter. The workshop description pushes against that simplification by asking for multifaceted evaluation across domains and perspectives. The difficulty is partly social: experts in security, social networks, ethics, and web mining often use different language and value different evidence. It is also technical: models and datasets can be judged by reliability, accessibility, fairness, privacy, semantic correctness, practical usefulness, and ethical risk, and these measures can disagree.
386.naive: A smart beginner would collect recent papers, sort them by topic, and summarize each abstract. That would produce a useful reading list, but it would not answer the deeper question: which claims should be trusted, compared, or used in practice? Abstract summaries usually repeat what authors say about their own work. They rarely explain how datasets shape conclusions, whether evaluation settings match real web systems, or how a security gain might trade against usability. Another simple approach is to rank methods by a single reported score. That fails because TIME's topics do not share one goal. Privacy, fairness, graph quality, web mining usefulness, and ethical acceptability cannot be collapsed into one number without hiding the reason that the comparison matters.
386.ap: The core idea is to treat evaluation itself as the object of study. Instead of asking only for new systems, TIME invites papers that step back and critically analyze models and datasets. A survey paper can organize scattered findings into a quick reference guide. An evaluation paper can compare how methods behave under different assumptions. A review paper can explain what a newcomer must understand before trusting a line of work. The workshop then adds invited talks from experts and industry leaders, so the written analyses are tested against practical experience from real web technologies. Mechanically, the central move is translation and comparison: take many specialized claims, expose the conditions behind them, make them accessible to researchers and practitioners, and turn them into actionable knowledge rather than leaving them as disconnected results.
386.mech: The mechanism begins with contributions from people who have examined a slice of web research deeply enough to compare it. The inputs are models, datasets, past results, and domain experience from areas named in the abstract: social networks, graphs, web mining, semantics and knowledge, security, privacy, fairness, and ethics. A submitted survey, evaluation, or review paper then transforms those inputs into a structured account. It may group methods by the problem they solve, identify the dataset properties that make results easier or harder, describe which assumptions are shared across papers, and point out where reported evidence is thin. The workshop setting adds a second transformation. Invited talks bring expert and industry perspectives, which can reveal practical constraints that papers alone may not show. Discussion and networking then compare the written evidence with lived deployment knowledge and expose disagreements. The output is not a trained model or a ranked list of systems. It is a set of reference guides, critical analyses, shared vocabulary, and practical guidance that help newcomers enter the field and help experienced researchers judge work across domain boundaries.
386.math: The mathematical idea behind this workshop is evaluation as structured comparison under many goals. A measurement is a rule for turning messy behavior into something comparable: a count, score, category, error rate, fairness gap, privacy risk, graph property, or qualitative judgment. The danger is that every measurement keeps some information and throws away the rest. Multifaceted evaluation exists because no single measurement can preserve all the parts that matter in web systems. This is the same tradeoff seen across the repo's concept data: ranking asks whose notion of better defines the order; similarity asks which differences can be ignored; probability asks how much confidence evidence deserves; network reasoning asks when links carry useful signal and when they mislead. TIME's contribution is not a new formula, but it is still mathematical in spirit. It asks authors to compare models and datasets along several axes, make assumptions visible, and explain why one kind of evidence should change belief in a claim. The useful operation is disciplined aggregation: gathering many observations without pretending they all measure the same thing or deserve equal weight.
386.dots: This paper connects to many neighboring conference ideas because it is about how those ideas are judged. Social network analysis and graph algorithms need evaluation that respects links, communities, and the risk that network structure can mislead. Web mining and semantics need evaluation that distinguishes useful patterns from artifacts of a dataset. Security and privacy need analysis of what information is protected and what useful signal remains. Fairness and ethics need evaluation that asks who benefits, who is harmed, and which historical patterns should not simply be repeated. In the repo's family context, TIME sits near social networks because the workshop includes that area, but its broader role is connective. It is a forum for comparing evaluation practices across families that usually appear separate: ranking, graph reasoning, knowledge representation, privacy, fairness, and trustworthy web systems.
386.ww: The approach works when the community's main bottleneck is not only inventing new methods but understanding the evidence around existing ones. A single paper can make a claim inside a narrow setup. A critical survey or evaluation can place that claim beside many others and ask what stayed constant, what changed, and what hidden condition might explain the difference. That comparison is powerful because repeated patterns across models and datasets reveal more than isolated success stories. Expert talks add another kind of check: deployment experience can expose costs, edge cases, and user harms that a paper's formal test may miss. The workshop format also helps newcomers because it compresses a large field into guided reference material without pretending the field is simple. It improves over the naive reading-list approach by organizing claims around assumptions, tradeoffs, and practical consequences, not just titles and method names.
386.po: The payoff is a better shared infrastructure for understanding web research. TIME promises quick reference guides for researchers and practitioners, better accessibility for newcomers, and distilled insights that can be turned into action. It also creates a meeting point for domain experts, research students, and industry leaders. If it succeeds, someone entering privacy, graph mining, fairness, security, or semantics can find a clearer map of what models and datasets have actually shown. Practitioners gain guidance that is closer to real constraints, while researchers get a venue where careful evaluation and synthesis count as first-class contributions.
386.limits: The abstract does not prove that the workshop will produce high-quality evaluations; it states the intention and the submission types. The value depends on accepted papers being genuinely critical rather than descriptive, and on invited talks adding evidence rather than general opinion. It also assumes that cross-domain discussion can overcome differences in vocabulary and evaluation goals across web mining, graphs, security, privacy, fairness, and ethics. Because this is a workshop description, it gives no selection criteria, examples of accepted analyses, or evidence that prior TIME outputs changed practice. The main assumption is that better synthesis can make a broad field more usable without flattening its tradeoffs.

387.bp: Industrial control systems (ICS)—power grids, water treatment, manufacturing—require safety-critical response times measured in tens of milliseconds. Security researchers often propose blockchain and encryption as panaceas. But if these slow down the control loop to hundreds of milliseconds, the system becomes unsafe. Real security must preserve the ability to respond in time.
387.wh: Blockchain consensus is inherently probabilistic—nodes negotiate agreement, introducing jitter. Homomorphic encryption (allowing computation on encrypted data) requires intensive computation, adding 100+ millisecond overhead. Industrial controllers need <10ms response time to be safe. The math is brutal: 51-440ms latencies violate safety-critical requirements by factors of 5-44x.
387.ap: This work analyzes where encryption overhead is incurred across the Purdue Model of industrial networks (Levels 0-5, from sensors to cloud). It shows BC+HE architectures create a 'dead zone' bottleneck at gateway levels, exposing vulnerabilities. The alternative: use lightweight lattice-based cryptography (LWE, Ring-LWE) for fast sensor-to-controller authentication (meeting <10ms constraints), and reserve BC+HE for non-real-time enterprise layers.
387.ww: Lattice cryptography is computationally cheap and quantum-resistant, making it suitable for real-time layers. Enterprise layers don't need microsecond response; they can absorb blockchain's latency. By decoupling security strategies by layer—speed for critical loops, richness for non-critical enterprise—the system achieves both safety and security without compromise.
387.po: The paper identifies a critical flaw in the BC+HE security paradigm for ICS: it can make systems unsafe. The lattice-based alternative preserves real-time safety while securing the network. This informs how ICS defenders should architect security without sacrificing responsiveness.

388.bp: LLM-enhanced search engines (ChatGPT, Gemini) are changing how people find information. They retrieve web content and synthesize answers, combining search's breadth with LLM reasoning. But attackers have learned SEO tricks over decades. Do these new systems fall for the old attacks, or do they deflect them better?
388.wh: Traditional search engines rank by links and keywords; attackers exploit both. LLM-enhanced search adds a new retrieval phase (finding relevant documents) and a ranking phase (deciding which sources matter). No one has systematically tested whether LLMSEs are vulnerable to known SEO attacks or if the LLM component acts as a defense.
388.ap: This work builds SEO-Bench, a dataset of 1,000 real-world black-hat SEO websites, and tests ten LLMSEs against them. They measure whether traditional SEO attacks (keyword stuffing, cloaking, link manipulation) work. They then propose new LLMSEO attacks: rewritten-query stuffing (rephrasing injection to evade detection) and segmented texts (hiding attacks across multiple retrieved documents). They measure manipulation rates on both.
388.ww: LLMSEs block traditional SEO attacks at the retrieval phase—the filter is strong. But the LLM reasoning phase can be fooled by attacks tailored to it. Rewriting queries to look like legitimate user intent, or fragmenting text so no single document looks suspicious but their union does, exploits the LLM's synthesis step. The system's new power creates new vulnerabilities.
388.po: The paper shows LLMSEs are robust against known SEO but vulnerable to LLMSEO variants—manipulation rates roughly double. This is the first systematic security analysis of LLM search, offering vendors concrete attack patterns to defend against and setting research direction for hardening these systems.

389.bp: Federated learning lets multiple parties train an AI model together without sharing raw data—banks collaborate on fraud detection, hospitals on disease prediction. But if one party wants to use a different model architecture (a smaller model on mobile, a larger one on desktop), the system breaks. Existing methods assume everyone uses the same model.
389.wh: Models are heterogeneous in practice: mobile clients can't run 500M-parameter networks. If a hospital uses a 1B-parameter model and a clinic uses 100M, how do they train together? Naive approaches ask everyone to use the global model, wasting resources on small clients and handicapping large ones. You need a way to federate across different architectures.
389.ap: FedBridge deploys a fusion model on each edge server that learns knowledge from heterogeneous client models via knowledge distillation (training the fusion model to mimic the client model's predictions). It uses a contrastive loss to align fusion model outputs with the global model, handling data heterogeneity. On the cloud server, a block-based aggregation merges fusion models from edge servers into a global model.
389.ww: Knowledge distillation lets a smaller or differently-shaped model pass its learned knowledge to another model without requiring them to share architecture. By intermediate fusion at edge servers, each client's model never needs to match others; they only need to communicate with their local edge fusion model. Block-based aggregation lets the cloud server combine fundamentally different models.
389.po: On public datasets with three different model architectures, FedBridge accelerates convergence 6.3x and improves accuracy 6.2%-17.7%, while cutting communication overhead 89.51%-96.13% and memory overhead 48.12%-61.77%. It enables federated learning across heterogeneous clients, making federation practical for real-world deployments.
